extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of science; philosophers of science; methodologists interested in the logic of induction and hypothesis-testing
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for forming, using, and judging scientific hypotheses and the legitimate use of the hypothetical method in scientific inquiry. Focuses on when hypotheses are permissible, what makes them testable/scientific, and how they should be used to guide induction, deduction, and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: “An hypothesis is any supposition which we make (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) in order to endeavor to deduce from it conclusions in accordance with facts which are known to be real.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are provisional suppositions intended to let us deduce consequences that can be compared with known facts; their primary purpose is explanatory — to enable the Deductive Method to be earlier applied to phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility by analogy with known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses that “ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature” possess plausibility; wholly arbitrary inventions of agents and laws lack that plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that posit causes or laws similar to those already known. Arbitrary fictitious agents with wholly novel laws are much less plausible and are rarely encountered in successful scientific history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must be capable of being proved or disproved by observed facts (verifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly scientific hypothesis should be “of such a nature as to be either proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a hypothesis cannot in principle be converted into a proved (or disproved) statement by reference to observations or experiments, it remains only a conjecture and should not be accepted as established science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa requirement (cause must be capable of independent detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause assigned, though not necessarily previously known, should be “capable of being known thereafter; that its existence should be capable of being detected, and its connection with the effect ascribed to it should be susceptible of being proved, by independent evidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke Newton’s maxim: the supposed cause must be a vera causa — something whose existence and causal power can be independently established. The ether example: plausible only insofar as independent evidence for such a medium could be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of the Hypothetical Method only when verification fulfils induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method suppresses induction and relies on ratiocination and verification; it is legitimate only if the verification “shall amount to, and fulfill the conditions of, a complete induction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothetical law may be assumed provided that, by deduction and subsequent verification, we can obtain the equivalent of full induction (i.e., show that no other law could produce the same verified consequences). Newton’s planetary reasoning is given as an example where verification functions as induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part discovery process: induction, ratiocination, verification — none dispensable
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover a cause by Deductive Method requires three parts: induction (ascertain laws of causes), ratiocination (compute from those laws), and verification (compare calculated effect with actual phenomenon). “No one of these three parts of the process can be dispensed with.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying or evaluating a hypothesis, check that these three components are present or that the verification legitimately substitutes for induction (see Method of Difference discussion). The moon/earth/gravity example is the canonical model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of both positive and negative instances (Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification must provide both the affirmative instance and the negative instance so that one can show no other antecedent would in conjunction with the background conditions produce the observed effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Difference requires showing A B C gives a b c and B C gives b c (positive and negative instances). Without the negative instance (showing other antecedents can't produce the effect), a hypothetical law is not securely established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses are legitimate heuristics if they suggest testable investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are indispensable in science as provisional suppositions which “put us on the road to that independent evidence” by suggesting observations and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to guide the choice of experiments and observations; begin with the simplest supposition consistent with the data and iteratively correct it (Methods of Approximation). Their value lies in leading to independent tests that can confirm or refute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: hypotheses that cannot be independently tested are unscientific
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses that cannot be brought to the test by any conceivable mode of observation or experiment (e.g., some formulations of Cartesian vortices) are defective because they cannot be converted to proved facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adopting hypotheses that do not suggest any plausible means of detection or disproof. The passage of comets through supposed vortices is cited as empirical disproof once testing was possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful prediction alone is not conclusive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The coincidence of predictions with subsequent observations, though impressive, “does not prove the reality of” the hypothesized mechanism; multiple coincidences could arise even if the underlying mechanism is different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat successful predictions as raising plausibility, not as definitive proof. Dr. Whewell’s argument (prediction = proof) is criticized: agreement of predicted and observed phenomena increases confidence but cannot by itself guarantee the truth of the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish cases where the cause is already ascertained from those where it is not
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inquiry is to determine the precise law of a cause already ascertained, the Hypothetical Method can attain negative instances and be legitimate; when the cause itself is wholly imagined to account for a, the assurance cannot be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the existence of the causal agent is already established (even if its law is not), hypothetical assumptions about the law are more defensible. If the agent itself is proposed without prior basis, greater skepticism and requirement of independent detectability are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the simplest initial hypothesis and iterate (Methods of Approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The simplest supposition which accords with the more obvious facts is the best to begin with; because its consequences are the most easily traced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with the simplest plausible hypothesis, trace its consequences, compare with facts, and correct iteratively. This heuristic aids tractability and progressive refinement toward non-hypothetical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses describing correspondences (not asserting causation) are acceptable when verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses that specify the law of correspondence between co-varying facts (even without causal claims) are legitimate provided false laws would lead to false results — e.g., Kepler’s attempts at laws of refraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such descriptive laws can be tested and, if they uniquely yield the observed relations, may be accepted even when causation is not asserted or known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: identical laws can arise from different mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of mathematical laws across phenomena (e.g., inverse square for gravitation, illumination, heat diffusion) does not imply identity of underlying mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer mechanistic identity merely from identical or similar formal laws. Maintain epistemic caution and seek independent evidence of mechanism beyond mathematical agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructive/historical inferences (geology, forensics) are legitimate forms of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring past causes from present effects (e.g., geological deposits or corpse evidence) is an inductive operation and is legitimate without gratuitous hypothesis when based on uniformities ascertained by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that certain sciences legitimately infer past events from present traces using induction grounded in known laws and analogies to observed processes; such inferences differ from speculative hypotheses about unknown agents.
